title: Fence Reason
question: You find a fence across an unused path and want it gone. What should you establish before removing it?
choices: The fence is there for a reason
The fence is old enough to ignore
The path is prettier without it
correctAnswer: The fence is there for a reason
correctExplanation: Right. Its purpose may not be obvious, so understand it before tearing anything down.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the fence is there for a reason. Structures often serve needs that are invisible until the day they are removed.
lessonContent:
Old arrangements may serve unseen purposes.
Investigate function before demanding change.
Absence of an obvious reason is not proof of none.
Ask who built this and what it protects.
Share this: question the purpose of one rule you dislike.

title: Look First
question: A reformer wants to abolish an institution immediately. What should come before any removal?
correctExplanation: Right. Diagnosis must precede surgery, or the operation damages what it meant to heal.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is understand before you remove. Acting fast on an unexamined target risks destroying something valuable.
lessonContent:
Diagnosis precedes treatment.
Understanding is cheap compared with regret.
Speed is not the same as progress.
Study the system before altering it.
Share this: learn the purpose of one thing before changing it.

title: Hidden Knowledge
question: An inherited custom seems arbitrary but has survived generations. What might it hold?
choices: Nothing at all of any value
correctExplanation: Right. Long-lived practices often encode solutions to problems we no longer remember facing.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is institutions store hidden knowledge. Survival across generations hints at a function worth discovering.
lessonContent:
Long survival suggests some usefulness.
Customs can carry forgotten lessons.
Before discarding, ask what problem it solved.
Treat inherited practice as evidence.
Share this: find the forgotten problem behind one tradition.

title: Diagnose First
question: A team blames every problem on one department and proposes dissolving it. What is missing?
correctExplanation: Right. Naming a culprit is not the same as understanding the cause of the trouble.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is reform needs a diagnosis first. Without knowing why something fails, dissolution may remove a needed function.
lessonContent:
Blame is not analysis.
A culprit is not necessarily a cause.
Find the mechanism before cutting it out.
Separate symptom from source.
Share this: separate one symptom from its actual cause today.

title: Ancient Solutions
question: A traditional practice looks inefficient but has never caused serious harm. What may it be?
choices: Tradition is a sign of ignorance
correctExplanation: Right. Ongoing practice may be quietly preventing a problem that reappears when it stops.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is tradition can encode solutions. What looks inefficient may be holding a risk at bay.
lessonContent:
Efficiency is not the only measure.
Some practices prevent invisible harms.
Absence of harm can be evidence.
Ask what would happen if it stopped.
Share this: consider the hidden benefit of one habit you keep.

title: Hasty Change
question: A policy is revoked quickly without testing it. What often follows?
correctExplanation: Right. Removing one part of a system usually shifts pressure somewhere unexpected.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is unintended consequences follow hasty change. Complex systems react in ways no quick reform anticipates.
lessonContent:
Systems push back when altered.
Effects ripple beyond the target.
Test small before changing everything.
Expect surprises and plan for them.
Share this: predict one side effect before making a change.

title: Who Must Prove
question: Someone wants to abolish a long-standing rule. Who carries the burden of proof?
choices: The burden of proof falls on the reformer
The burden of proof falls on the rule
No proof is needed at all
correctAnswer: The burden of proof falls on the reformer
correctExplanation: Right. The person proposing the change must show why it is an improvement.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the burden of proof falls on the reformer. Existing arrangements get the benefit of the doubt until a case is made.
lessonContent:
Change is not automatically progress.
Whoever proposes a change argues for it.
The default deserves a charitable reading.
Demand reasons, not just enthusiasm.
Share this: ask for the case behind one proposed change.

title: Chestertons Rule
question: A principle warns against removing a structure before you know why it was built. What is it called?
correctExplanation: Right. You should only clear an obstacle once you understand its original purpose.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is Chestertons fence principle. It counsels comprehension before demolition, not reverence for everything old.
lessonContent:
Named principles compress practical wisdom.
Comprehension should precede removal.
Obstacles may be protections in disguise.
Learn the history before you act.
Share this: apply one cautionary principle to a change you plan.

title: Locked In Choices
question: Why can a poor layout persist even after everyone agrees it is poor?
correctExplanation: Right. Early decisions shape what is easy to change later, so inferior arrangements can survive.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is path dependence locks in choices. Each step built on the last makes reversal costly, regardless of quality.
lessonContent:
History constrains present options.
Early choices raise the cost of later change.
What is stuck may still be improvable.
Look for the decisions that locked things in.
Share this: find one trapped choice and ask what locked it.

title: Load Bearing
question: A policy seems to do nothing useful but removing it causes collapse elsewhere. What was it?
choices: What looks pointless may be load bearing
What looks pointless is always pointless
What looks pointless was an accident
What looks pointless is a lie
correctAnswer: What looks pointless may be load bearing
correctExplanation: Right. A piece can hold the whole structure up while appearing entirely idle.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is what looks pointless may be load bearing. Function is not always visible from the outside.
lessonContent:
Visible idleness can hide essential support.
Removal is a test that reveals function.
Test on a small scale if you must.
Assume support until proven otherwise.
Share this: identify one quiet element holding a system together.

title: Visible Function
question: A reformer notices only the obvious purpose of an institution and ignores the rest. What is the risk?
choices: Reformers see only the visible function
correctAnswer: Reformers see only the visible function
correctExplanation: Right. Institutions usually do several jobs, and the loudest one is not always the most important.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is reformers see only the visible function. Hidden roles go unprotected when change targets only the obvious one.
lessonContent:
Organisations serve multiple purposes.
The obvious role may be the least vital.
Ask what else this does for people.
Protect functions you did not set out to touch.
Share this: name a second job done by one familiar institution.

title: Local Knowledge
question: A central planner replaces a local practice with a uniform rule. What is often lost?
correctExplanation: Right. The people closest to a situation hold details that no distant plan can capture.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is local knowledge beats central plans. Uniform rules can override context-specific solutions that worked well.
lessonContent:
Context-specific detail resists central design.
People on the spot know their constraints.
Uniform rules can erase working solutions.
Consult those closest to the problem.
Share this: ask a local expert for a detail no plan accounts for.

title: Time Reveals
question: Why might an old, tested practice be more trustworthy than a clever new one?
correctExplanation: Right. Long use exposes failures that a designer cannot foresee at a desk.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is time reveals what design cannot. Survival through many real conditions is a form of evidence.
lessonContent:
Real-world testing beats theory alone.
Survival across conditions is evidence.
New does not automatically mean better.
Weigh track record against promise.
Share this: compare one new idea with an older proven alternative.

title: Small Steps
question: A reform can be done all at once or in stages. What does the caution suggest?
choices: Incremental change is safer than wholesale
correctAnswer: Incremental change is safer than wholesale
correctExplanation: Right. Staged change lets you see effects and correct course before too much is altered.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is incremental change is safer than wholesale. Smaller steps keep the door open to adjustment and reversal.
lessonContent:
Staged change preserves the option to correct.
Small steps reveal effects early.
All-at-once change forecloses adjustment.
Keep reversibility where you can.
Share this: split one big change into a testable first step.

title: Past Survivors
question: A practice has outlasted many attempts to replace it. What does this survivorship suggest?
choices: Survivors of past tests deserve respect
correctAnswer: Survivors of past tests deserve respect
correctExplanation: Right. Lasting through repeated challenges is weak but real evidence of usefulness.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is survivors of past tests deserve respect. What endures has passed trials that alternatives did not.
lessonContent:
Survival is a form of testing.
What endures has met many challenges.
Respect is not the same as worship.
Investigate why it persists.
Share this: ask why one longstanding practice keeps returning.

title: Forgotten Conflicts
question: A rule seems to make life harder for no visible gain. What might it be preventing?
choices: Rules exist only to annoy people
Rules are always written by mistake
correctExplanation: Right. Many rules are the residue of disputes that would flare again if the rule vanished.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is rules often resolve forgotten conflicts. Their cost is visible while the harm they prevent is not.
lessonContent:
Rules can be solutions to old disputes.
The conflict may be invisible now.
Cost of compliance is easier to see than avoided harm.
Ask what would return if the rule went.
Share this: find the old conflict behind one annoying rule.

title: Removed Support
question: Taking away a small guideline causes problems in unrelated places. What does this reveal?
choices: Removing a support reveals its role
Nothing can be learned from it
correctAnswer: Removing a support reveals its role
correctExplanation: Right. A quiet rule may be holding several things together in ways nobody noticed.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is removing a support reveals its role. Function becomes apparent only when the element is withdrawn.
lessonContent:
Removal is a diagnostic test.
Quiet elements can support many parts.
Watch distant effects to find a role.
Learn structure from what breaks.
Share this: notice what changes when one small support is gone.

title: Novelty Trap
question: A team assumes anything newer must be superior to what it replaces. What is the error?
correctExplanation: Right. Being recent says nothing about being better; only results can show that.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is novelty is not improvement. Recency is a description, not a measure of quality.
lessonContent:
Freshness and quality are separate traits.
New things can be worse than what they replace.
Judge by outcomes, not by date.
Resist fashion in decisions.
Share this: evaluate one new thing by results rather than novelty.

title: Context First
question: A solution that worked in one place fails somewhere else. What should guide the decision?
choices: Failure means the theory is wrong
correctExplanation: Right. The same rule works differently depending on the conditions around it.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is context matters more than theory. A general model must be adapted to the particular setting.
lessonContent:
General rules meet particular conditions.
What works here may fail there.
Adapt before transplanting.
Study the receiving environment.
Share this: adapt one general tip to your specific situation.

title: Pilot Test
question: Before rolling out a new policy everywhere, what does a cautious approach recommend?
choices: Test changes on a small scale first
correctAnswer: Test changes on a small scale first
correctExplanation: Right. A trial run surfaces problems cheaply before they affect everyone.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is test changes on a small scale first. Pilots contain the cost of mistakes and inform the full rollout.
lessonContent:
Small trials contain the cost of error.
Learn before committing everything.
Measure the result against a comparison.
Scale only what works.
Share this: pilot one change before applying it broadly.

title: Who Built It
question: Before judging an old practice as absurd, what question should you ask?
choices: Ask who built this and why
Ask how to remove it fastest
correctAnswer: Ask who built this and why
correctExplanation: Right. Knowing the original problem and builder clarifies whether the practice still serves a need.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is ask who built this and why. Understanding the origin turns a mystery into a decision about present relevance.
lessonContent:
Origins explain present form.
Understand the problem before judging the answer.
Designers faced constraints you may share.
History informs current choices.
Share this: learn the origin of one practice in your life.

title: Bad Rules
question: A rule is genuinely flawed yet persists. What might still be true of it?
choices: Even bad rules can do useful work
Bad rules help no one ever
correctAnswer: Even bad rules can do useful work
correctExplanation: Right. An imperfect rule may yet provide stability or coordination worth preserving in a replacement.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is even bad rules can do useful work. Reform should carry over the function, not just remove the fault.
lessonContent:
Faults and functions can coexist.
Reform should keep what works.
Total removal may lose hidden benefits.
Replace rather than merely delete.
Share this: identify a useful function inside one flawed rule.

title: Preserve Function
question: You replace an old rule with a better one. What should the new rule aim to keep?
choices: Reform should add as much as possible
correctExplanation: Right. The point is to fix the flaw while retaining the job the old rule was doing.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is reform should preserve function. Skipping this step repeats the original error in reverse.
lessonContent:
Change should keep the good.
Identify the function before replacing it.
Reform is surgery, not demolition.
Check that the new version still works.
Share this: state the function a change must preserve.

title: Invisible Reasons
question: Why is it hard to judge whether an old arrangement should stay or go?
correctExplanation: Right. The original rationale may never have been documented and the context is long gone.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is historical reasons are often invisible. Missing records force careful inference rather than assumption.
lessonContent:
Reasons may never have been recorded.
Context disappears before explanations do.
Infer purpose from effects.
Ask people who remember.
Share this: recover the reason behind one undocumented practice.

title: Reversible Steps
question: When uncertain about a change, what property makes it safer to attempt?
choices: Reversibility is a virtue in reform
correctAnswer: Reversibility is a virtue in reform
correctExplanation: Right. A step you can undo allows learning without locking in the consequences.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is reversibility is a virtue in reform. Keeping options open reduces the cost of being wrong.
lessonContent:
Undoable decisions are cheaper to try.
Reversibility limits downside risk.
Keep exits open under uncertainty.
Prefer steps you can retract.
Share this: design one change so it can be undone.
